author: Codex
scope: Research entities, units of analysis, Gem Finder measures and score interpretation. A shared reference for the laboratory; distinct from the Topic atlas’s topic vocabulary.

categories.title: Gem Finder measures
categories.description: Six assessed qualities, one computed distance and observed word count. No combined gem score.

categories.title: Research entities & units
categories.description: Evidence hierarchy, analysis roles, counting rules and source provenance.

entries.title: Conversational surprise
entries.definition: How much a passage departs from the conversational direction established by its immediate context.
entries.practical: Use this to find changes of frame, challenges to assumptions and abrupt redirections. Read the preceding messages: surprise belongs to a passage-in-context, not to a sentence on its own.
entries.low: An echo, agreement or nearby elaboration of the established idea.
entries.high: A challenge to the framing, or a change in the organizing question or mode of exchange.
limits: This is a rubric judgment of local departure, not token surprisal, statistical rarity or worldwide originality.
Unexpected does not mean valuable. A generic reset or incoherent interruption can depart sharply from the preceding exchange.
entries.example: After several turns designing a memory system, ‘What would you like to talk about today?’ can be a surprising reset with little contribution. ‘What would make us decide to stop preserving this memory?’ may both redirect the exchange and open a useful question.

entries.title: Conceptual contribution
entries.definition: How much an articulated explanation, distinction, synthesis or question helps reorganize or clarify the issue under discussion.
entries.practical: Use this to find passages that offer something you can think with: a mechanism, a distinction, a consequence, or a question that makes competing explanations easier to separate.
entries.low: An assertion or paraphrase that does not explain what it changes.
entries.high: A developed mechanism, synthesis or discriminating question that shows what follows from its framing.
limits: The rating concerns the articulated idea, not verified truth or historical originality.
High contribution can occur without surprise: a careful answer may develop the existing question rather than redirect it.
entries.example: ‘Memory matters’ asserts a theme. ‘If every memory records what would disconfirm it, the archive becomes a tool for revising beliefs’ offers a mechanism and consequence. The mechanism still needs scrutiny.

entries.title: Creative connection
entries.definition: How far a passage develops a meaningful relationship between distinct ideas, perspectives or domains.
entries.practical: Use this to find analogies that do explanatory work. Look for explicit correspondences and for a new implication, question or limit derived from the connection.
entries.low: Ideas are merely named together, or an analogy is offered without showing how it works.
entries.high: Specific correspondences support a further implication or reveal where the analogy breaks down.
limits: Unusual juxtaposition alone does not establish a useful connection.
A familiar analogy can score highly if well developed. The score does not establish that nobody has made the connection before.
entries.example: ‘Conversation is a garden’ names an analogy. Linking questions to seeds and replies to growing conditions, then asking which conversational habits crowd out new ideas, develops the analogy into an investigable question.

entries.title: Expressive force
entries.definition: How effectively the wording makes an idea vivid, perceptible or memorable.
entries.practical: Use this to find phrases worth keeping and images that make a difficult distinction easier to grasp. Check whether the wording helps you understand, rather than only producing an impression of depth.
entries.low: Routine, formulaic or indistinct phrasing; plain wording can also fall toward the lower levels.
entries.high: Precise phrasing or a developed image makes a nuanced distinction graspable and meaningfully quotable.
limits: Beauty, persuasiveness and memorable wording do not establish correctness.
Plain, accurate prose can be useful with modest expressive force; ornate language alone is not sufficient for a high rubric level.
entries.example: ‘We kept moving, but the map never changed’ can make the difference between activity and progress memorable. Its expressive force depends on the surrounding idea, and does not prove that no progress occurred.

entries.title: Conceptual complexity
entries.definition: How extensively a passage develops interacting conceptual relationships, conditions, tensions or levels of explanation.
entries.practical: Use this to locate passages that work through systems of relationships. Compare with substance to see whether those relationships are made inspectable, and with contribution to see what they clarify.
entries.low: No developed relationship, or a single simple relation or unqualified claim.
entries.high: A structured system of interacting relationships, feedback, tensions or limits is worked through.
limits: Complexity is descriptive, not automatically desirable. A simple insight can be a gem.
The rubric asks for developed relationships, not word count or jargon. The assessor may still show length or style effects; this pilot does not establish their absence.
entries.example: ‘Feedback improves learning’ states one relation. Explaining how feedback changes confidence, confidence changes exploration, and exploration changes the evidence available develops an interacting system—even if the account later proves mistaken.

entries.title: Substance & specificity
entries.definition: How well explicit reasoning, examples, distinctions or developed images support the passage’s own meaning.
entries.practical: Use this to separate inspectable claims from vague profundity. Ask whether you can identify the claim, the support offered and, at higher levels, a boundary or consequence that would distinguish it from alternatives.
entries.low: Vague or circular language, or an identifiable claim whose key connection remains unspecified.
entries.high: Explicit reasoning or detail supports an identifiable meaning and states a boundary, counterexample or discriminating consequence.
limits: This measures textual support and specificity, not external factual accuracy. A detailed invented formula can be inspectable and still invalid.
Abstract or poetic writing can have substance. Concrete-sounding vocabulary is not enough by itself.
entries.example: ‘Everything is interconnected’ is hard to inspect. Naming which signals affect which decisions, and a condition under which the effect would disappear, adds substance. Evidence is still needed to establish that the described effect exists.

entries.title: Topic-profile distance
entries.definition: How far a passage’s broad-topic score pattern lies from its nearest comparable patterns in other conversation lineages.
entries.scale: 0–100 · distance units on the broad-topic score scale
entries.formula:
d(a,b) = √[Σⱼ(aⱼ − bⱼ)² / 24]
D(a) = mean of the 5 smallest lineage-minimum distances
method: Represent a passage by its 24 broad-topic JEV scores, each on 0–100. Compute root-mean-square (RMS) difference from each eligible reference passage.

Exclude its own lineage. Within each other lineage, keep only the nearest passage; take the five nearest distinct lineages and average their distances. Fewer than five eligible lineages means unknown.
The frozen pilot reference contains 8,371 eligible passages from 376 development lineages. The 60 reserved validation lineages are excluded from targets, context and reference.
The reference is frozen. UI filters change which passages you see, not the reference pool or a passage’s stored distance.
entries.practical: Use this to find unusual mixtures of assessed topics relative to this corpus. Open the saved neighbors to see what the score considers close; similar topic patterns can occur in very different wording.
entries.low: A broad-topic score pattern close to patterns found in other lineages.
entries.high: A pattern farther from its five nearest lineage neighbors; unusual within this reference set.
limits: Distance is not a percentile or the probability of being a gem. A distance of 18 does not mean the 18th percentile or an 18% chance.
This is topic-profile rarity, not linguistic originality, local conversational surprise or quality.
The result depends on the topic vocabulary, JEV assessments and reference composition. Changing these would define a new comparison.
entries.example: Two passages about cognition and philosophy may have nearly identical profiles despite very different arguments. A passage combining cooking, logistics and ritual may be more distant in this corpus without being insightful.

entries.title: Word count
entries.definition: The number of whitespace-separated units in the target passage, used to explore whether passage length is associated with Gem ratings.
entries.scale: Nonnegative integer · actual words; no 0–100 rescaling
method: The count is already recorded for every assessed Gem passage and is computed the same way for reader-selected examples. It counts the visible target reply alone, excluding supplied context, prompts and separately recorded reasoning.

Python split() separates on whitespace and ignores empty pieces. Punctuation remains attached to its chunk; an isolated symbol can count as a unit. This is a reproducible length proxy, not linguistic word segmentation.
Word count is an eighth plotting axis, not a seventh JEV question. It requires no model call. The matrix, pair correlations, sorting and length filters use the original count.
Plots give word count its own range. Minimum and maximum filters are inclusive. Choosing a histogram bin saves its boundaries in the URL; changing to a different pair preserves that word interval.
entries.practical: Use word count on the horizontal axis and contribution, expression, complexity or substance on the vertical axis. Look for brief passages with high ratings, then filter to a comparable length range and, where possible, the same model. Read the passages and save your own judgment.
entries.low: A shorter visible reply. A concise formulation can be beautiful or illuminating with few words.
entries.high: A longer visible reply, with more room for elaboration, examples and developed relationships. Length alone does not establish quality.
limits: A word is not a tokenizer token. Token counts depend on the model/tokenizer and can include hidden reasoning or different accounting; this axis does not estimate them.
Whitespace counts are less comparable across languages without regular word spacing, code and formulas.

A length–score correlation could reflect real elaboration, assessor preference for verbosity, model/topic differences or their mixture. It does not by itself identify a causal confounder or prove bias.
The lab does not divide ratings by words or silently adjust scores. Length restriction supports exploration; it is not a complete statistical adjustment or independent validation.
entries.example: A short sentence can make a distinction memorable, while a longer reply spells out several relationships. A higher complexity rating for the longer reply may describe that structure accurately without making it the more beautiful passage.

entries.title: Scaled rubric score
entries.definition: The assessor’s expected rubric level, rescaled from 0–4 to 0–100 for display.
entries.formula:
Expected level = Σₖ k × P(level k), k = 0,…,4
Displayed score = 25 × returned expected level
method: Each Gem rating has five ordered criteria. TypeSafe returns a distribution over those levels and a Score. The lab displays the returned Score × 25.
The raw level probabilities are retained without renormalization. Small rounding differences from the returned Score are tolerated by the frozen parser.
These numbers treat successive rubric levels as equally spaced. Comparing differences is a modeling convention, not a calibrated physical measurement.
entries.practical: Read a score beside its rubric and distribution. A score of 75 corresponds to expected level 3; it does not mean a 75% chance that the passage is a gem.
limits: Equal means can conceal different uncertainty. Scores on different axes refer to different criteria, not interchangeable units of merit.
No composite gem score or universal quality threshold is defined.
entries.example: Half the probability on level 2 and half on level 4 gives an expected level of 3 (75 displayed). All probability on level 3 has the same mean but a different distribution. These are illustrative distributions.

entries.title: Level probabilities & confidence
entries.definition: Level probabilities describe the assessor’s distribution over the five rubric criteria. Confidence is a separate provider-returned field, shown alongside them.
entries.scale: Level probabilities and confidence: 0–1, displayed as percentages
method: Gem Finder shows the returned probability for each rubric level and the returned confidence. It does not compute a new confidence statistic.

The current UI describes confidence as concentration across levels. The five-level distribution is the directly inspectable evidence of how the assessment is spread; no formula for the provider confidence field is specified by this lab.
entries.practical: Inspect the probability bars to distinguish a concentrated assessment from one spread over several levels. Use uncertain or conflicting cases for closer reading and rubric refinement.
limits: Confidence is not a probability that the idea is true, novel or worth keeping.
A confident assessor can be wrong. Calibration against independent human judgments remains pending.
entries.example: An expected level near 2 can reflect a strong preference for level 2 or a split between low and high levels. The mean alone hides that difference.

entries.title: JEV topic probability
entries.definition: JEV’s assessment of whether the target satisfies a particular topic question, displayed on a 0–100 scale.
method: The JEV Topic Atlas asks explicit semantic questions about target passages. Its Boolean probability is different from the Gem Finder’s expected five-level Score.
Broad and specific topic questions may overlap. Candidate thresholds such as ≥80 select passages for exploration; their shares do not form mutually exclusive topic proportions.
entries.practical: Use topic scores to navigate candidate passages and compare distributions, then read the target and question. Broad scores also form the vectors used for Gem topic-profile distance.
limits: A returned probability is a model assessment, not established calibration against human truth.
A passage can score highly on several topics. Scores do not sum to 100 across topics.

entries.title: Pearson correlation (r) & pair count (n)
entries.definition: Pearson r summarizes linear association between two displayed measures. n counts passages with both current scores in that matrix cell.
entries.formula: r = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² × Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²]
method: Use the currently filtered passages with both finite scores and current source text. Missing and stale scores are omitted separately for each pair; observed zeros remain.
The lab displays r only with at least three pairs and variation on both axes. The matrix rounds displayed r to two decimals.
entries.practical: Positive r means the measures tend to rise together; negative r means one tends to fall as the other rises. Inspect the scatter for clusters and outliers that the summary can hide.
limits: r near zero does not rule out a nonlinear relationship. Correlation does not establish causation.
These are descriptive development-sample associations. Length, model, topic, common assessor and sample selection can all contribute; they are not adjusted for here.
entries.example: Contribution and complexity can rise together because useful explanations develop more relationships, because the assessor rewards length, or because of the sampled model mixture. The correlation alone cannot decide among these accounts.

entries.title: Full scale & observed ranges
entries.definition: Two ways to display the same values: fixed 0–100 ranges for ratings and distance, or narrower observed ranges. Word count always keeps its own range in actual words.
method: Full scale uses 0–100 for ratings and profile distance; words use zero to a rounded upper count. Observed ranges narrow each axis to its filtered values, rounding scores to multiples of ten and words to a scale-appropriate integer step. Constant axes retain a nonzero span; empty word axes show 0–10.
Each measure uses the same range throughout its matrix row and column. The ten diagonal histogram bins divide that displayed range; the last bin includes its upper endpoint.

The focused-pair histogram uses ten fixed 10-point bins for scores and ten equal-width integer word bins for length. An active word bin retains its width as other filters change or another pair is opened; counts outside that retained histogram range are reported. Clear the bin to rescale.
Display-range changes do not recalculate values or correlations. Word count is never clipped to 100 or converted into a rating.
entries.practical: Observed ranges make narrow spreads, especially topic-profile distance, easier to inspect. Full scale helps you see how much of the possible score range the sample actually occupies.
limits: A visually large gap after zooming may be a small numeric difference. Read the printed axis bounds.
Histogram bar shapes can change with the display range and binning; the underlying observations do not.

entries.title: Unknown, unscored & stale
entries.definition: A dash means there is no usable current score. It is different from an observed score of zero.
method: A score is usable only when it is numeric, finite and its passage source is current. A reader-selected example can be available to read but have no JEV assessment.
Plots omit missing values; pair counts require both scores. Sorting places missing values last. A changed source withholds its old scores and saving until resolved.
entries.practical: Check n before comparing cells. An unscored passage is still available for your own reading; it has not received a negative assessment.
limits: Missingness may be selective. Do not silently treat absent assessments as low scores.

entries.title: Gem & personal reading
entries.definition: A gem is a passage you judge worth keeping. The six model ratings and topic distance provide routes to discovery, rather than deciding that judgment for you.
method: Your verdict, note, optional exact quotation and optional six axis ratings are saved as Local researcher, separately from JEV’s scores and Codex development readings.
Updates preserve revision history. The record notes whether model scores were hidden in that view; earlier exposure is not controlled.
entries.practical: Keep examples of what works and what falls flat, with your reason. Disagreements with the scores help identify what the rubric is missing and inform a future version.
limits: There is no validated universal extraordinary score, combined ranking or automatic gem threshold.
Hiding scores is useful for reading, but does not by itself create a blinded, independent validation study.

entries.title: Broad profile lead
entries.definition: The broad topic with the highest recorded score for a passage, used as a Gem Finder filter.
method: Choose the maximum among the passage’s broad-topic scores. This is a convenient navigation label; the full vector remains available for computing distance.
The lead does not require the maximum to pass a candidate threshold, and does not erase other high topic scores.
entries.practical: Use the filter to browse passages with a similar leading profile, while remembering that their topic mixtures may be quite different.
limits: The lead is not a reviewed initial topic, a mutually exclusive topic assignment or evidence that the dialogue stayed on that topic.
A low or nearly tied maximum is still a maximum; read the actual scores when the distinction matters.

entries.title: Conversation
entries.definition: One initiated dialogue with a participant roster, experimental setup and recorded history. Its history can include alternative continuations.
entries.practical: Say 48 messages from 48 conversations when each selected reply came from a different dialogue. Count the dialogue separately from its messages.
method: Conversation membership is established from its recorded run and source identity. Topic changes do not create new conversations.
A conversation can have more than two participants, external interventions or an incomplete ending. Its setup and status remain attached.
limits: A technical run or synthetic fixture must not silently become a real conversation in a scientific denominator.
A new branch or a repeated assessment of a reply does not create an independent conversation.

entries.title: Run
entries.definition: A recorded execution with a setup and outcomes. A conversational run contains a dialogue; a technical run records an integration or qualification check.
entries.practical: Use runs for library totals that include both conversations and technical checks. State which kinds are included before comparing counts.
method: The catalog identifies a run with run_id. A campaign journal can contain several run roots; a source file is not necessarily one run.
The population banner currently counts started nonsynthetic runs, with synthetic fixtures and unstarted slots reported separately.
limits: An unfinished or short run is still a run. It is not automatically an eligible conversation for every analysis.

entries.title: Message
entries.definition: One recorded contribution by a regular conversation participant. It may contain one sentence or many paragraphs.
entries.practical: Use message as the countable unit for whole replies. A selected full reply in Mind & discourse or Gem Finder is still a message.
method: Locate a message using its run/conversation ID, message ID and source revision. Identical text generated at different positions remains distinct evidence.
A capped or partial output remains a recorded message with a status flag. Visible reply text and separately recorded reasoning are fields of the record; they do not add two participant messages.
limits: A scheduled position without an available reply is not an observed message. Empty recorded text, missing output and partial output need explicit eligibility rules.
External interventions have their own role and must not be folded into regular participant-message counts.

entries.title: Turn / scheduled position
entries.definition: A position in the conversation schedule at which a participant is expected to contribute.
entries.practical: Use turn numbers to locate the sequence. Use message IDs to identify actual evidence, especially in branched conversations.
method: A turn can remain pending, be blocked or have an unresolved response. Scheduled positions and recorded messages therefore have different denominators.
Turn numbers may recur across branches. The term does not mean a pair of replies or a complete multi-participant round.
limits: Do not convert planned turns into observed messages or treat missing output as a negative topic result.

entries.title: Excerpt
entries.definition: An explicitly bounded selection of text within one recorded message.
entries.practical: Use excerpt for a quoted sentence or selected paragraph; use message when the whole recorded reply is the object being analyzed.
method: Preserve the source run, message ID, source revision, exact quotation and start/end boundaries. Current saved span checks use Python string positions (Unicode code points), not bytes.
A multi-message selection needs explicit ordered membership and boundaries. It must not be inferred from an unqualified passage label.
limits: Several excerpts from one message are not independent replies. New excerpt scoring requires its own declared assessment unit.

entries.title: Branch & conversation path
entries.definition: A branch is an alternative continuation from an existing point in a conversation. A path follows one ordered history through that conversation.
entries.practical: Read a message along its actual path. Count shared earlier messages once when summarizing unique messages across branches.
method: Where ancestry is recorded, message parent IDs identify the actual path. A linear transcript can instead carry one ordered history.
The context builder follows recorded ancestry and includes intervening external events.
limits: Two branches sharing earlier messages are not two independent dialogue histories. Turn number alone cannot identify a branch message.

entries.title: Transcript
entries.definition: The recorded representation of a conversation or one selected path through it.
entries.practical: Open the transcript to read selected messages in their surrounding dialogue and inspect the recorded setup.
method: A transcript view can contain participant messages and external events. Display choices must retain their roles.
Alternative transcript views and exports can represent the same underlying conversation.
limits: A transcript file or another rendering does not automatically create an additional conversation or experimental replicate.

entries.title: External intervention
entries.definition: An event introduced from outside the regular participant roster to affect a conversation.
entries.practical: Distinguish an external model disrupting a dialogue from a third model participating in its regular exchange.
method: Record the external role, event kind, source/model, content and position where available. Historical recipient labels such as X or Y do not by themselves establish participant status.
An intervention can enter the context for a later message while remaining separate from regular participant-message counts.
limits: An external contribution does not automatically increase the number of regular participants. Missing historical metadata stays unknown.

entries.title: Conversation lineage
entries.definition: The laboratory grouping used to keep shared ancestry and identical recorded conversation structures together for sampling and comparison.
entries.practical: Use lineage to recognize related evidence when sampling or splitting development and validation data. Several messages from one lineage share history.
method: The current coverage inventory computes its grouping from models, prompt and recorded message structure, including IDs, parents, speakers, text and status. It preserves the frozen rule; it is not a newly verified historical genealogy.

The original Gem pilot selects one message per lineage. Its expansion permits up to three across both samples. Profile neighbors exclude the target lineage and use at most one neighbor from each other lineage.
limits: Distinct run IDs do not necessarily establish distinct lineages. A source-run count must not be relabeled as a lineage count.
Different lineages can share models, prompts and experimental conditions. Distinct ancestry alone does not establish statistical independence.

entries.title: Campaign
entries.definition: A group of runs organized under an operational plan, with a defined scope and execution rules.
entries.practical: Use campaign to identify how related runs were generated, then inspect each run and its actual outcomes.
method: Retain the protocol, model/configuration identities, allocation and outcome records used by that campaign.
A campaign can contain several conversational roots and conditions. A journal can store more than one run.
limits: A campaign is not necessarily one conversation, one model or one experimental condition.

entries.title: Study / research collection
entries.definition: A curated grouping of evidence and findings around a research question. It can gather conversations from different campaigns.
entries.practical: Use a study to keep relevant conversations, observations and notes together without changing the source evidence.
method: Collection membership is a saved selection. It does not create new source conversations.
Keep the collection purpose, membership and attributed findings separate from the execution plan that generated the data.
limits: A research collection is not automatically a randomized experiment or representative sample.

entries.title: Analysis target
entries.definition: The object selected for a particular analysis: a message, an excerpt or a whole conversation, as declared by that method.
entries.practical: Read target as selected for assessment. In current Mind & discourse and Gem samples, the targets are messages; target is not an extra textual level.
method: Record the target unit, source identity, exact selected content and selection method. Current message targets retain run_id, message_id and source_sha256.
Repeated wording conditions, question packs or assessors evaluate the same target without adding messages to its sample.
limits: Future excerpt-level or conversation-level scoring needs a declared unit and procedure. Existing scores must not silently be reinterpreted at those levels.

entries.title: Context / assessment window
entries.definition: Additional evidence supplied to an assessor to help interpret the selected target. A window comprises that target and its declared context.
entries.practical: Check what the assessor could see before interpreting a score. The context does not add extra targets to the sample.
method: Gem Finder inherits the corpus target window: the selected message plus up to two preceding evidence events on its actual path. These can include participant messages or external interventions. Mind & discourse currently supplies only the selected message text.
The source plan fixes the exact context policy and text. Later replies and the full conversation are not implied by a local window.
limits: The same message assessed with different context can yield different results. Context policies from different assessment versions must not be merged silently.

entries.title: Assessment sample
entries.definition: The set of target identities selected under a stated sampling rule for an assessment.
entries.practical: Report the number and kind of selected objects, such as 48 messages, and separately how many conversations supplied them.
method: Frozen samples preserve target membership, source revisions, selection rules and exclusions. Multiple assessments of an existing target do not enlarge that sample.
Different samples may include the same message. Their counts cannot simply be added without checking identities.
limits: A development sample or availability-limited selection is not automatically representative of the full library.

entries.title: Analysis dataset
entries.definition: A defined set of analysis units together with their metadata and measurements at a specified revision.
entries.practical: Choose the dataset before interpreting a filter count. A message table and a conversation summary have different units even when they use the same evidence.
method: Record the unit of analysis, source/assessment versions and dataset fingerprint. Current corpus analysis joins question packs to the same message identity.
A dataset can cover a full eligible frame or a selected sample. Loading a new score snapshot is distinct from filtering existing rows.
limits: Rows with different units cannot be pooled as if each were one message. Overlapping datasets are not disjoint populations.

entries.title: Filtered subset
entries.definition: The part of the selected sample or dataset that satisfies the active population filters.
entries.practical: Read the current subset against its named base, for example 3 messages from a 48-message assessment sample.
method: Population counts cover all matching units before pagination. Sorting, choosing visible features or changing display style alone does not create a smaller population.
Topic thresholds, model, length and other actual filters may restrict the subset. A separate cell selection for close reading can be smaller still.
limits: A threshold-selected subset is not a new independently sampled experiment. State unknown-score handling and the denominator used for percentages.

entries.title: Unit of analysis
entries.definition: The kind of object represented by one observation in an analysis: for example a message, an excerpt or a conversation.
entries.practical: State the unit with every count and percentage. Messages, conversations, assessments and feature scores answer different counting questions.
method: Declare the unit, target identity, eligibility rules, dataset/sample and actual filters. If messages are aggregated by conversation, state the aggregation rule.
A message-level table can contain repeated observations within each conversation. Experimental assignment and statistical dependence must be specified separately from the displayed row unit.
limits: A distinct row does not establish an independent experimental replicate. Branches share prefixes; messages share history; conversations can share model and setup.

entries.title: Assessment
entries.definition: An evaluation of a selected object under a specified assessor, instrument version, wording, context and procedure.
entries.practical: Keep the assessed message count separate from the number of evaluations. Four wording conditions evaluate one message four ways.
method: Link assessments to their target identity and exact question/context specification, assessor model and recorded outcomes.
An assessment can produce a vector of feature scores. Operational question packs may require more than one request to assemble that vector.
limits: More assessments do not create more independent messages. A failed call provides no valid score and does not establish a negative label.

entries.title: Feature / assessment question
entries.definition: A feature is a dimension to assess, such as a topic or discourse pattern. A question specifies how the instrument operationalizes that dimension.
entries.practical: A row can have 27 feature scores while still representing one assessed message. Different wording can change how a feature is measured.
method: Preserve stable feature/question IDs, definitions, wording conditions and instrument versions alongside results.
Features may overlap or all be absent. A feature family groups dimensions for navigation or a specified summary.
limits: A familiar feature name alone does not guarantee that different instruments measure the same construct.

entries.title: Score / measurement result
entries.definition: The recorded value for one defined measure on an analysis unit, with its scale and provenance.
entries.practical: Distinguish a JEV yes-probability, a Gem expected rubric level and a derived mean. They can share a display range while answering different questions.
method: Interpret an assessed score with its target, feature, assessor and procedure. Derived summaries also need an explicit calculation and coverage count.
Missing results remain unknown; observed zero remains a value. A score vector contains several measurements of the same unit.
limits: Score count is not message count. A high value does not by itself establish truth, originality, calibration or personal value.

entries.title: API request & attempt
entries.definition: A logical request specifies an intended API payload. An attempt is a recorded dispatch of that request; it can succeed, fail or remain unresolved.
entries.practical: Use request and attempt counts to understand execution and cost. Use message counts to describe the evidence sample.
method: A request may bundle many feature questions, or a question set may be divided into packs. Allowed retries add attempts without creating new target messages.
Keep payload identity, response/receipt, status, usage and retry authorization attached to the frozen execution plan.
limits: Request, assessment, score and target counts need not be equal. Unknown-cost outcomes must not be interpreted as free or successful.

entries.title: Synthetic control text & fixture run
entries.definition: A synthetic control text is an authored input used to examine a classifier. A synthetic fixture run is constructed execution data used to test the software.
entries.practical: Keep classifier controls separate from model-generated conversation messages and from engineering fixtures. They serve different purposes.
method: Mind & discourse contains Codex-authored control texts alongside its separate transcript sample. Synthetic fixture runs are a different library category.
Keep origin, author and intended check attached to constructed evidence, and use separate denominators.
limits: An intended positive or negative control is not independent human validation. Synthetic data must not be counted as observed model behavior.

entries.title: Source artifact & revision
entries.definition: A source artifact is an original file, journal or response receipt. Its revision is the particular version identified by a checksum or other recorded identity.
entries.practical: Use source artifacts to trace a displayed message or score back to evidence. Do not use source-file totals as conversation totals.
method: Preserve artifact bytes, source hashes and stable run/message references. One journal can represent several runs; several artifacts can document one run.
The population banner currently uses source records for distinct run IDs. That display label does not count files or another unit inside a conversation.
limits: Changing a display name does not change source identity. If source text changes, an old score must not silently attach to the new text.

entries.title: Passage (legacy term)
entries.definition: An older reading label whose precise unit depends on the saved method. In the current Gem Finder and Mind & discourse samples, a target passage is one selected recorded message.
entries.practical: When a count says passages, check the method. Use messages for whole recorded replies and excerpts for explicit text selections. Use target to describe which object is being assessed.
method: The former combined Target passage & preceding context entry is now separated into Message, Analysis target and Context entries. This stable passage link remains available.
Historical plans and exact assessment questions retain their original wording. This terminology guide does not change their text, boundaries or IDs.
limits: Passage alone does not specify a paragraph, full message, excerpt or context window. It should not be used as an unspecified counting unit.
